title: One public address, many private machines
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how many machines share one public address, predict which connections NAT allows and which it blocks, and name the techniques used to work around it.

blocks.text: Your home network probably has a dozen devices and one public address. Every connection any of them makes appears to the outside world as coming from that single address. The device doing the translation keeps a table, and almost everything surprising about home and corporate networking follows from how that table works.
The translation, and the table behind it

blocks.caption: What the router rewrites, and what it remembers
lines: The router rewrites the source and records the mapping:
the router looks it up, rewrites the destination, and delivers it.
/* The port number is what makes one address serve many machines:
each connection gets its own outside port. */

blocks.text: Why incoming connections do not work

The table is built by outgoing traffic. A packet arriving from outside, for a connection nobody inside started, matches no entry — and the router has no way to know which of the twelve machines it was meant for. So it is dropped.

blocks.title: NAT is not a firewall, but it behaves like one by accident
blocks.text: Blocking unsolicited inbound traffic is a side effect of not knowing where to send it, not a security decision. It is genuinely useful, and it is not a substitute for a firewall: it does nothing about outbound traffic, nothing about traffic between machines inside, and nothing once a mapping exists. Treat it as a consequence to be aware of rather than a control you are relying on.

rows: Someone connecting to your laptop from outside
Two machines behind different NATs connecting directly
A video call between two home users
A manual rule: this outside port always goes to that inside machine
Both sides send outbound at the same moment, each creating a mapping the other can use
Both sides connect outward to a server in the middle, which forwards between them
The inside machine holds an outbound connection open for the outside to use

blocks.text: Every one of those works by making the connection outbound from the perspective of the NAT. That is the general principle: if you cannot receive, connect outward and keep it open. It is why almost every remote-access product on the market is built around a persistent outbound connection rather than an inbound one.

blocks.title: Carrier-grade NAT: your provider does it too
blocks.text: Many providers now put whole neighbourhoods behind shared public addresses because IPv4 addresses ran out. That means you may not have a public address at all — port forwarding on your own router will not help, because there is a second layer of translation above it that you do not control. If forwarding is configured correctly and still does not work, check whether your address is inside 100.64.0.0/10, the range reserved for exactly this.

items: Every mapping is state, so a router has a finite number of simultaneous connections it can track
Idle mappings are eventually discarded, which is why long-lived connections send keepalives
Protocols that put addresses inside their own messages need the router to rewrite those too, which is why some old protocols need special handling
Diagnosing across a NAT is harder: the address a server sees is not the address of the machine that sent the traffic

blocks.title: Watch translation happen
steps: Find your private address: ip addr show   and note it
Find the address the world sees: curl -s https://api.ipify.org ; echo
Compare them — if they differ, everything you send is being translated
Check whether you are behind carrier-grade NAT: is your address inside 100.64.0.0/10?
Run: ss -tn state established | head    and note your local ports
Open several connections at once (a few curl commands) and watch how many local ports are in use
If you control a router, look at its NAT or connection-tracking table while doing this
On a Linux router or with root: conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | head    (the table itself)
blocks.expected: Two different addresses for the same machine, and a set of local ports that each map to a different outside port. If the two addresses are the same you have a public address, which is increasingly unusual for a home connection and worth knowing about your own network either way.

cheatsheet: NAT rewrites the source address and port on the way out, and reverses it on the way back
The port number is what lets one public address serve many machines
The mapping table is built by outgoing traffic only
Unsolicited inbound traffic matches no entry and is dropped
That inbound blocking is a side effect, not a security control — do not rely on it as one
Port forwarding is a permanent manual mapping
Hole punching, relays and reverse tunnels all work by making the connection outbound
Carrier-grade NAT puts you behind a second layer you do not control: check for 100.64.0.0/10
Mappings are state and expire — long-lived connections need keepalives
curl https://api.ipify.org shows the address the world sees

checkpoint.prompt: Twelve devices at home share one public address. What distinguishes their connections at the router?

choices.B: A different outside port number for each connection, recorded in a mapping table
choices.D: The order the connections were made

checkpoint.explanation: One address plus many ports is what makes the sharing possible. Each entry maps an outside port back to a specific inside address and port.

checkpoint.prompt: Is it accurate to say NAT protects your network like a firewall?

choices.C: No — inbound traffic is dropped because the router does not know where to send it, and that side effect covers nothing else

checkpoint.explanation: It genuinely does block unsolicited inbound traffic, which is useful. But it does nothing about outbound traffic, traffic between inside machines, or anything once a mapping exists.

checkpoint.prompt: A video call connects two users who are both behind home routers. How?

choices.A: Both send outbound at the same moment, each creating a mapping the other's traffic can use
choices.C: The call always goes through a central server
choices.D: One of them must have a public address

checkpoint.explanation: With a relay server as the fallback. Every technique for traversing NAT works by making the connection outbound from each side's point of view. Relaying is the fallback when that fails, not the first choice, because it costs the provider bandwidth.

checkpoint.prompt: You configure port forwarding correctly and it still does not work. What should you check?

choices.C: Whether your provider is using carrier-grade NAT

checkpoint.explanation: Check for an address inside 100.64.0.0/10. A second layer of translation above your router cannot be configured from your side. That reserved range is the specific sign that you are behind one.
